summary: Describes how to use the L2TPv3 control plane for Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM) pseudowires, and gives guidelines for carrying various ATM services over an IP network. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4454 describes how to carry ATM circuits, the fixed-size cells that classic ATM networks use, across an IP network using L2TPv3 tunnels. The two ends set up a session for each circuit and then send the traffic in one of two ways: either as reassembled AAL5 packets, or as individual ATM cells. A small extra header carries the congestion and priority bits that the cells carried, and signalling messages tell the far end when the circuit goes up, down or into alarm.

what is the atm specific sublayer
subtitle: How to carry ATM circuits across an IP network as L2TPv3 pseudowires, in packet or cell form.

tldr.problem: L2TPv3 could carry layer 2 services over IP, but there was no defined way to carry Asynchronous Transfer Mode circuits, so ATM links could not be extended across an IP network.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines the signalling, the encapsulation and a new ATM-specific sublayer for L2TPv3 sessions, and gives two ways to carry the traffic: reassembled AAL5 packets, or raw ATM cells.
tldr.outcome: An ATM virtual circuit can now be tunnelled over IP, with the state of the circuit and its alarms signalled between the two ends. RFC 4454 was later updated by RFC 5641.

today: RFC 4454 was published in May 2006 as a Proposed Standard and has since been updated by RFC 5641. It remains the reference for carrying ATM circuits over L2TPv3.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Layer 2 Tunneling Protocol, Version 3 defines an extensible tunneling protocol to transport layer 2 services over IP networks. This document describes the specifics of how to use the L2TP control plane for Asynchronous Transfer Mode pseudowires, and provides guidelines for transporting various ATM services over an IP network.

The document covers using L2TP for ATM pseudowires, including encapsulation, carrying various ATM services such as AAL5 SDU and ATM VCC, VPC and port cell relay over L2TP, and mapping ATM defects to L2TP Set-Link-Info messages to notify the peer L2TP Control Connection Endpoint. Any ATM-specific AVPs or other L2TP constructs for ATM pseudowire support are defined here as well. Support for ATM switched virtual paths and connections, and for soft permanent virtual paths and connections, are outside the scope of this document. The reader is expected to be very familiar with the terminology and protocol constructs defined in RFC 3931.
sections.plainLanguage: ATM is the cell-based technology that older carrier networks used. This document makes it possible to carry those cells over an IP network inside an L2TPv3 tunnel, so a circuit can span two networks that speak different things.

sections.title: Session Establishment, Teardown and Maintenance
sections.content:
To emulate ATM pseudowires using L2TP, an L2TP control connection as described in RFC 3931 MUST be established. The Start-Control-Connection-Request and the corresponding reply MUST include the supported ATM pseudowire types in the Pseudowire Capabilities List, which identifies the control connection as able to establish L2TP sessions in support of the ATM pseudowires. An endpoint MUST be able to identify itself uniquely in those two messages via a globally unique value, by default the structured Router ID AVP, though the unstructured Hostname AVP MAY also be used.

Creation of an ATM circuit, for example an AAL5 PVC, triggers establishment of an L2TP session using the three-way handshake described in RFC 3931. An endpoint MAY initiate the session immediately upon circuit creation, or wait until the circuit state transitions to ACTIVE, which delays the allocation of resources until it is really needed. The Circuit Status AVP MUST be present in the Incoming-Call-Request and Incoming-Call-Reply messages, and MAY be present in the Set-Link-Info message.

The signalling needs a Pseudowire Type AVP, holding one of 0x0002 for ATM AAL5 SDU VCC transport, 0x0003 for ATM cell transport port mode, 0x0009 for ATM cell transport VCC mode, or 0x000A for ATM cell transport VPC mode. It also needs a Remote End ID, which identifies the ATM circuit at the far end and MUST be present in the Incoming-Call-Request so that the remote endpoint can associate the session with the circuit. The Remote End Identifier AVP is of opaque form, though implementations MAY simply use a 4-octet value known to both ends. How that value is configured or discovered is outside the scope of the document.

The Incoming-Call-Reply is sent only after the ATM circuit transitions to ACTIVE. If the far end has not been provisioned for the circuit, a Call-Disconnect-Notify is returned immediately, and the initiating end SHOULD then use a periodic retry mechanism whose period and maximum number of retries MUST be configurable. An implementation MAY send the request or the reply before a PVC is ACTIVE, as long as the Circuit Status AVP reflects that the circuit is INACTIVE and a Set-Link-Info message is sent when the circuit becomes ACTIVE. The Incoming-Call-Connected is the final stage of session establishment, confirming receipt of the reply with acceptable parameters so that traffic can flow in both directions.

When an ATM circuit is unprovisioned at either end, the associated L2TP session MUST be torn down with the Call-Disconnect-Notify message. All sessions established by a given control connection use the L2TP Hello facility for session keepalive, which gives basic dead peer and path detection between the endpoints. After the initial establishment, the Set-Link-Info control message signals ATM circuit status between the endpoints, including ACTIVE or INACTIVE notifications, and it MUST be sent whenever there is a status change that may be reported by any value in the Circuit Status AVP. The only exceptions are the initial request, reply and disconnect messages. The Set-Link-Info message is also used to map ATM OAM or physical layer alarms into the Circuit Status AVP.
sections.plainLanguage: Each ATM circuit gets its own tunnel session, set up with a three-message handshake. After that, a control message is used whenever the circuit's state changes, so both ends always know whether it is up.

sections.title: Encapsulation and the ATM-Specific Sublayer
sections.content:
The general encapsulation format for ATM services over L2TP has four parts: the PSN transport header, which is specific to IP and its underlying transport header and carries the encapsulated payload through the IP network; the session header, a non-zero 32-bit session ID with an optional cookie of up to 64 bits, exchanged during session setup; the ATM-specific sublayer; and the ATM service payload.

The ATM-specific sublayer is REQUIRED for AAL5 SDU mode and OPTIONAL for ATM cell mode. It is an alternative to the default L2-specific sublayer, and it defines four new flag bits, T, G, C and U, alongside the existing S bit and the B and E fragmentation bits. If the B and E bits are not used, they MUST be set to 0 on transmission and ignored on receipt.

The T bit indicates whether the packet contains an ATM admin cell or an AAL5 payload. If T is 1, the packet contains an ATM admin cell, encapsulated according to the VCC cell relay encapsulation. The G bit is the explicit forward congestion indication: the ingress endpoint SHOULD set it to 1 if the EFCI bit of the final cell of the incoming AAL5 payload is set, or of the single cell being carried, and the egress endpoint SHOULD set the EFCI bit of all outgoing cells to that value. The C bit carries the cell loss priority in the same way, and the egress endpoint SHOULD apply it to all outgoing cells.

The U bit is the command or response bit. When FRF.8.1 Frame Relay and ATM PVC service interworking traffic is being transported, the least significant bit of the AAL5 CPCS-PDU user-to-user octet may contain the Frame Relay command or response bit, and the ingress endpoint SHOULD copy that bit to the U bit, with the egress endpoint copying it back.

An additional enumeration is added to the L2-specific sublayer AVP to identify the sublayer: 0 means no L2-specific sublayer is present, 1 means the default one is used, and 2 means the ATM-specific sublayer is used. The first two values were already defined in the L2TPv3 base specification.

Data packet sequencing MAY be enabled for ATM pseudowires, using the mechanisms described in RFC 3931 to signal sequencing support. ATM pseudowires over L2TPv3 MUST request the presence of the ATM-specific sublayer when sequencing is enabled, and MAY request its presence at all times.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet carries a small extra header with four flags. One says the packet holds an admin cell rather than user data, one carries the congestion bit, one carries the priority bit, and one carries the Frame Relay command bit.

sections.title: ATM Transport and OAM Cells
sections.content:
There are two encapsulations supported for ATM transport. The ATM-specific sublayer is prepended to the AAL5 SDU. The other, cell mode encapsulation, consists of the optional ATM-specific sublayer followed by a 4-byte ATM cell header and a 48-byte ATM cell payload.

In AAL5-SDU mode, each AAL5 virtual channel is mapped to an L2TP session. The ingress endpoint reassembles the AAL5 CPCS-SDU without the AAL5 trailer and any padding bytes. Incoming EFCI, CLP and command or response bits are carried in the ATM-specific sublayer across the pseudowire to the egress endpoint. If the ingress endpoint finds that an encapsulated AAL5 SDU exceeds the MTU size of the session, the SDU may be fragmented as described in RFC 3931 or under the transport layer. F5 OAM cells that arrive during the reassembly of an AAL5 SDU are sent immediately on the pseudowire followed by the AAL5 SDU payload, and in this case the relative order of OAM cells with respect to user data cells is not maintained. Performance monitoring OAM cells and security OAM cells should not be used with AAL5 SDU mode, and these cells MAY be dropped at the ingress endpoint because cell sequence integrity is not maintained. The Pseudowire Type AVP, attribute type 68, MUST be present in the Incoming-Call-Request and MUST include the ATM AAL5 SDU VCC transport type of 0x0002.

In ATM cell mode, cells skip the reassembly process at the ingress endpoint. They are transported over an L2TP session, either as a single cell or as concatenated cells in a single packet. Each ATM cell consists of a 4-byte header and a 48-byte payload, and the header error checksum is not included. The ATM-specific sublayer is OPTIONAL in this mode, and it can be included if sequencing support is required. The maximum number of concatenated cells in a packet is limited by the MTU size of the session and by the ability of the egress endpoint to process them.

Three cell relay services are defined. The VCC cell relay service maps an ATM virtual channel connection to a single pseudowire using cell mode, with the ATM cell transport VCC mode type of 0x0009. The VPC cell relay service maps an ATM virtual path connection to a single pseudowire, with the type 0x000A. The ATM port cell relay service allows an ATM port to be connected to another ATM port, encapsulating all cells received at the ingress ATM port into a pseudowire PDU, with the type 0x0003. Each endpoint MUST discard any idle or unassigned cells received on an ATM port associated with ATM pseudowires.

OAM cells are always encapsulated using cell mode encapsulation, regardless of the encapsulation format used for user data. For VCC switching, the endpoints SHOULD be able to pass the F5 segment and end-to-end fault management, resource management, performance management, activation and deactivation, and system management OAM cells. F4 OAM cells are inserted or extracted at the virtual path link termination and are not sent across the pseudowire. For VPC switching, the endpoints MUST pass F4 and F5 OAM cells transparently.
sections.plainLanguage: In one mode the ATM data is put back together into ordinary packets before it is tunneled. In the other, each 53-byte cell is carried through unchanged, so nothing about the cell order is lost.

sections.title: The New Attribute Value Pairs
sections.content:
Three new AVPs are defined. The ATM Maximum Concatenated Cells AVP, attribute type 86, indicates that the egress endpoint can process a single PDU with concatenated cells up to a specified number of cells. An endpoint transmitting concatenated cells on the pseudowire MUST NOT exceed the maximum number of cells specified in this AVP. It applies only to the ATM cell relay pseudowire types, and its value may differ in the two directions of the pseudowire. The attribute value is a single octet, the AVP length before hiding is 8, and it MAY be hidden. It is sent in the Incoming-Call-Request and Incoming-Call-Reply during session negotiation, or via Set-Link-Info control messages when the endpoint changes its configuration. It is OPTIONAL, and if the egress endpoint is configured with a maximum number of cells to be concatenated it SHOULD signal that value.

The OAM Emulation Required AVP, attribute type 87, may be needed to signal OAM emulation in AAL5 SDU mode if an endpoint cannot support the transport of OAM cells across L2TP sessions. If OAM cell emulation is configured or detected on one side, the other endpoint MUST support it as well. It is exchanged during session negotiation or over the life of the session via Set-Link-Info control messages. If the other endpoint cannot support OAM cell emulation, the L2TP session MUST be torn down with a Call-Disconnect-Notify carrying result code 22. This AVP is boolean, with no attribute value: its absence is false and its presence is true. Its length before hiding is 6.

The ATM Alarm Status AVP, attribute type 88, indicates the reason for the ATM circuit status and the specific alarm type, if any, to the peer endpoint. It is an OPTIONAL AVP that may be present in the Set-Link-Info message with the Circuit Status AVP. The Circuit Status Reason is a 2-octet unsigned integer and the Alarm Type is also a 2-octet unsigned integer, so the AVP length before hiding is 10 octets. The Circuit Status Reason values are 0 reserved, 1 no alarm or alarm cleared, which is the default for an active status, 2 unspecified or unknown alarm received, the default for an inactive status, 3 to 7 for an F1 to F5 alarm received on the ingress endpoint, 8 for the circuit down because of an ATM port shutdown on the peer endpoint, and 9 for the circuit down because of a loop-back timeout on the ingress endpoint. The general alarm types are 0 reserved, 1 no alarm type specified, 2 Alarm Indication Signal, 3 Remote Defect Indicator, 4 Loss of Signal, 5 Loss of Pointer, 6 Loss of Framer, 7 loopback cells and 8 Continuity Check.
sections.plainLanguage: Three extra control fields. One tells the far end how many cells it may pack into one packet, one says that operations cells have to be emulated rather than carried, and one explains why the circuit changed state.

sections.title: Applicability of the Two Modes
sections.content:
ATM pseudowires operate in a point-to-point deployment model, and support two modes of encapsulation, AAL5-SDU mode and cell relay mode. ATMPWs operating in AAL5-SDU mode only support the transport of PVC-based services. The AAL5 CPCS-PDU from a single VCC is reassembled at the ingress endpoint and the AAL5 CPCS-SDU, that is the CPCS-PDU without its trailer or PAD octets, is transported over the pseudowire. Segmentation and reassembly functions are therefore required at the endpoints. There is a one-to-one mapping between an ATM PVC and an ATMPW operating in AAL5-SDU mode, supporting bidirectional transport of variable length frames. With the exception of optionally transporting OAM cells, only ATM Adaptation Layer type 5 frames are carried in this mode.

Because the ATM cell headers and the AAL5 CPCS-PDU trailer are not transported, several things are lost. The EFCI and CLP values of individual ATM cells that constitute the AAL5 frame may be lost, and CLP and EFCI transparency is not maintained. Only the least significant bit of the CPCS-UU field in the trailer is transported, using the ATM-specific sublayer, and applications that transfer user-to-user information using that octet would fail to operate. The CPI field in the trailer is also not transported. The trailing CRC field in the CPCS-PDU is stripped at the ingress endpoint and not transported, and is regenerated at the egress endpoint instead. Since the CRC has end-to-end significance, errors introduced during encapsulation or transit across the packet switched network may not be detected, so the L2TPv3 session can use IPsec to keep payload integrity checking transparent.

The status of the ATM PVC is signalled between the endpoints using the Circuit Status AVP, with more granular cause values and specific alarm types signalled using the ATM Alarm Status AVP, and loss of connectivity detected by the L2TPv3 keepalive mechanism. F5 OAM cells that arrive during the reassembly of an AAL5 SDU are sent immediately over the pseudowire and before the AAL5 SDU payload, so applications that rely on cell sequence integrity between OAM and user data cells may not work. Fragmentation and reassembly procedures MAY be used for mismatched MTUs, and the procedures described in RFC 3931 can be used to support the maximum size of an AAL5 SDU, 65535 octets. Relying on fragmentation of the L2TP over IPv4 packet between the tunnel endpoints limits the maximum size of the AAL5 SDU, because the maximum total length of an IPv4 datagram is already 65535 octets, and the maximum AAL5 SDU is then limited to 65535 minus the encapsulating headers, 24 to 36 octets for L2TP over IPv4 or 36 to 48 octets for L2TP over UDP and IPv4.

In cell relay mode, no reassembly takes place at the ingress endpoint and there are no segmentation and reassembly requirements for the endpoints. ATM-layer cells are transported over the pseudowire, so all AAL types can be carried. The cells consist of a 4-byte ATM cell header and a 48-byte cell payload, and the service payload of a cell relay mode pseudowire is a multiple of 52 bytes. The header error checksum, a CRC over the first 4 bytes of the cell header, is not transported, so errors in the header introduced during encapsulation or transit may not be detected, and again IPsec can be used to keep integrity checking transparent. Cell concatenation improves bandwidth efficiency but introduces latency and delay variation. OAM cells are transported in the same fashion as user cells and in the same order as they are received, so applications that rely on cell sequence integrity between OAM and user data cells are not adversely affected. Fragmentation and reassembly are not used for cell relay pseudowires, because concatenating cells and then fragmenting the result acts as an inverse function with a null net effect.
sections.plainLanguage: Choosing the mode is a trade-off. Reassembling packets is efficient but loses the per-cell bits and the end-to-end checksum. Carrying cells untouched keeps everything but costs more overhead and cannot be fragmented.

sections.title: Congestion Control
sections.content:
The packet switched network carrying the pseudowire may be subject to congestion, with characteristics depending on the type of network, its architecture, its configuration and its loading. During congestion the network may show packet loss and packet delay variation that will impact the timing and data integrity of the pseudowire. During intervals of acute congestion, some cell relay pseudowires may not be able to maintain service.

Whenever possible, cell relay pseudowires should be run over traffic-engineered networks providing bandwidth allocation and admission control. IntServ-enabled domains providing Guaranteed Service, or DiffServ-enabled domains using Expedited Forwarding, are examples of traffic-engineered networks, and such networks will minimize loss and delay while providing some degree of isolation of the pseudowire's effects from neighbouring streams.

If the network provides a best-effort service, the best-effort congestion avoidance considerations apply. Pseudowires that carry constant bit rate and variable bit rate real-time services will most probably not behave in a TCP-friendly manner. In the presence of services that reduce their transmission rate, such pseudowires SHOULD be halted when acute congestion is detected, in order to allow other traffic to continue. Pseudowires carrying unspecified bit rate traffic, which is equivalent to best-effort IP service, need not be halted and MAY have cells delayed or dropped by the ingress provider edge if necessary. Pseudowires carrying variable bit rate non-real-time services may or may not behave in a TCP-friendly manner, but are most likely safe to continue operating, since the end-user application is expected to be delay-insensitive and may also be somewhat loss-insensitive.

Endpoints SHOULD monitor for congestion, for example by measuring packet loss, to ensure that the ATM service may be maintained. When severe congestion is detected, the ATM service SHOULD be terminated by tearing down the L2TP session with a Call-Disconnect-Notify message. The pseudowire may be restarted by manual intervention or by automatic means after an appropriate waiting time.
sections.plainLanguage: Real-time traffic does not slow down when the network gets busy, so it has to be stopped instead. The document says which kinds of traffic to halt first and which to keep going.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: ATM over L2TPv3 is subject to the security considerations defined in RFC 3931. There are no additional considerations specific to carrying ATM that are not present when carrying other data link types.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing extra is needed for ATM. The general L2TPv3 security rules cover it.
